summary: Describes the policy, authorization and enforcement requirements for choosing which services get applied to a given OPES data flow. It focuses on who may decide which edge services act on traffic, and how those decisions are enforced.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3838 sets out who decides which Open Pluggable Edge Services are applied to a given flow. A rule author writes the rules, an administrative service checks and compiles them, and the device in the data path applies them to each message. The memo also sets out what users and publishers are each entitled to ask for, and what has to be encrypted on the way.

questions: who decides which edge services apply to traffic
what is a policy decision point
what is a policy enforcement point
what are the opes rule processing points
subtitle: Who decides which edge services act on a user's traffic, and how that decision is made and enforced

tldr.problem: Under OPES a network device can apply services to the traffic passing through it, but nothing said who chooses those services, who may veto them, or how a user finds out what has been applied to them.
tldr.mechanism: The memo splits policy into three parts: a rule author who supplies the rules, a Policy Decision Point that authenticates the author and compiles the rules, and a Policy Enforcement Point in the data path that evaluates each message against the compiled rules and calls the services.
tldr.outcome: The requirements give users the right to see, change and block the services applied to their traffic, give publishers their own say, and require encryption and integrity protection between the pieces wherever user data crosses a trust boundary.

facts.label: Policy components
facts.value: 3: Rule Author, Policy Decision Point and Policy Enforcement Point

facts.label: Privacy limitations a user may set
facts.value: 4: hide identity, hide profile, no traffic to third-party callout servers, no traffic from particular sites

facts.label: Every OPES service must have
facts.value: A unique name, cryptographically bound to the entity responsible for the service

today: RFC 3838 is an Informational memo from August 2004 that has not been obsoleted or updated. It states requirements for OPES policy, authorisation and enforcement rather than describing a protocol, and its own security considerations section points to RFC 3837 for the security and privacy issues of OPES services.

sections.title: What OPES Policies Are For
sections.content:
The Open Pluggable Edge Services architecture enables cooperative application services between a data provider, a data consumer and zero or more OPES processors. The application services under consideration analyse and possibly transform application-level messages exchanged between the data provider and the data consumer. The OPES processor can distribute the responsibility of service execution by communicating and collaborating with one or more remote callout servers, and the execution of such services is governed by a set of rules installed on the OPES processor. Rule evaluation can trigger the execution of service applications local to the processor or on a remote callout server.

Policies express the goals of an OPES processor as a set of rules used to administer, manage and control access to resources. The requirements in this document govern the behaviour of OPES entities in determining which of the available services are to be applied to a given message, if any.

The scope of the policies described is limited to those that describe which services to call and, if appropriate, with what parameters. They do not include policies that prescribe the behaviour of the called services themselves. It is desirable to enable a common management framework for specifying policies for both the calling of and the behaviour of a service, and the integration of such a function is the domain of policy administration user interaction applications.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo is about the choice of services, not about what the services do once chosen. It asks who writes the rules, who checks them, who applies them, and what a user is allowed to say about the result.

sections.title: The Policy Components
sections.content:
The policy functions are decomposed into three components: a Rule Author, a Policy Decision Point, and a Policy Enforcement Point. The Rule Author provides the rules to be used by an OPES entity, and these rules control the invocation of services on behalf of the rule author. The decision point and the enforcement point interpret the collected rules and appropriately enforce them.

The decision point provides for the authentication and authorisation of rule authors and the validation and compilation of rules. The enforcement point resides in the data filter, where the data from an OPES flow is evaluated against the compiled rules and appropriate calls to the requested services are performed.

The interface between rule authors and the policy decision points must use the format that may result from the requirements in this document. The interface between the decision point and the enforcement point can be internal to a specific vendor implementation, but implementations must use a standard interface only if the two reside on different OPES processors. Splitting the two apart permits the offloading of some tasks to an administrative service located on a server separate from the real-time enforcement services on the processor. The decision point must be a service that provides administrative support to the enforcement points, it must authenticate the rule authors, it must verify that the specified rules are within the scope of the rule author's authority, and it must be a component of the OPES Administration Authority.

At the enforcement point, rules may chain actions together, where a series of services to be called are specified, and the implementation must ensure the passing of information from one called service to another. The implementation must not prohibit the re-evaluation of a message to determine whether another service or set of services should be called. Executing an action may modify message property values, for example a service that converts JPEG images to GIF images modifies the content type of the requested web object, and such modification may change the behaviour of subsequently performed actions. The data filter should act on matched rules before it evaluates subsequent rules, and multiple matched rules can be triggered simultaneously if the filter can determine in advance that there are no side effects from any of them. A data filter may evaluate messages several times in the course of handling a flow, and the rule processing points may be defined by administratively defined names, which can serve as a selector for policy rules.

Four commonly used processing points are identified by the numbers 1 to 4 in the message flow between a data consumer application, an OPES processor and a data provider application: the data consumer request handling role, which processes a request when it is received from the data consumer application; the OPES processor request handling role, which processes a request before forwarding it to the data provider application; the data provider response handling role, which processes a response when forwarding it to the data consumer application; and the OPES processor response handling role, which processes a response when forwarding it to the data consumer application. Any data filter or any administrative implementation must support the four rule processing points.
sections.plainLanguage: Somebody writes the rules, an administrative service checks and compiles them, and the device in the path applies them. The rules are checked at four moments: when a request arrives, before it is sent on, when a response arrives, and before it is sent back.

sections.title: Requirements for the Interfaces
sections.content:
The interface between the policy system and the OPES services must be able to pass system state information as well as the subject message. The invoked OPES services must be able to be specified in a location independent fashion, so the rule authors need not know and need not specify the instance of a service in the rules. The rule author should be able to identify the required service at the detail level appropriate to their needs, by specifying a type of service or any service that fits a general category of service to be applied to their traffic.

The binding of service names to a specific service may be distributed between the decision point and the enforcement point, and as rules are compiled and validated they must be resolved to a specific installation's set of homogeneous OPES services. The selection of a specific instance may be postponed and left to the enforcement point, at rule installation time or at run time, and to achieve interoperability the enforcement point must support resolving a generic name to a specific instance, which it is possible to do with services such as SLP or UDDI. The policy system may support dynamic discovery of service bindings, the required binding information must be provided by the decision point and conveyed on the enforcement point interface, and a service description methodology such as WSDL must be present in the policy system.

There may be a need for a means of maintaining state information used in both condition evaluation and action execution, and depending on the execution environment, OPES services may have the freedom to define variables they need and use these to define their behaviour further. Policy rules may specify that state information be used as part of the evaluation of the rules against a given message, so the policy system should support the maintenance of groups that can be used in evaluating rule conditions, with membership in such groups used as action triggers. The example given is an authorised site blocking service: rather than calling the service for each request sent by a blocked user, a rule determines whether a user is a member of blocked users and whether a requested site is a member of blocked sites, and then invokes a local blocking service. Environment variables can also pass state information between services, for instance where an analysis of the request or modifications to it need to be captured and passed to other services on the request path or on the responses associated with it.

On rule management: rule providers must be authenticated and authorised for rules that apply to their network role, must not be able to specify rules outside their scope of authority, and should be able to specify only what is needed for their services. Compilation of rules from different sources must not lead to the execution of conflicting rules, and the resolution of such conflicts is out of scope. Rules are assumed to be static and applied to current network state. It is desirable to choose standard technologies such as XML for the rule language format, while the mechanisms for sending rules from the rule authors to the administrative server, and from there to the processor, are out of scope.

Rule conditions must be matched against attribute values of the encapsulated protocol as well as environment variable values, and attribute values include protocol header values and possibly protocol body values. The rule system should allow unconditional rules rather than requiring rule authors to specify conditions that are always true, which some services such as logging need. The rule system must allow the specification of rule actions that are triggered if the conditions of a rule are met, and rule actions must identify the OPES service to be executed for the current message request or response. Rule actions may contain run-time parameters which control the behaviour of a service, and if specified these must be passed to the service that is executed.

Finally, on policy expression: the OPES processor must enforce the policy requirements set by data consumers and publishers, and cannot do this consistently unless there is an unambiguous semantics and representation of the data elements mentioned in the policy. The examples given are of a user asking that his identity not be shared with other OPES administrative trust domains and later finding his family name shared, or finding that a different part of a web form had to be filled out to protect the family name. The policy must therefore have definitions of data elements, their relationships and how they relate to enforcement, and these semantics must be agreed by all OPES service providers. Users must be assured that they can know their settings, change them if the provider's policy allows, and have reasonable assurance that they are enforced with reasonable interpretations.
sections.plainLanguage: Rules name services in general terms, and the system works out which particular server to call. Rules can match on the message itself, on state the system keeps, or on nothing at all, and each rule names the service to call and the parameters to call it with.

sections.title: Authenticating People and Authorizing Services
sections.content:
An OPES rule determines which attributes of traffic will trigger the application of OPES services. The author of the service can supply rules, but the author cannot supply the necessary part of the rule precondition that determines which network users will have the services applied for them. An OPES service provider must satisfy five major requirements: allow all users to request the addition, deletion or blocking of OPES services for their traffic, where blocking means do not use this service for my traffic; prevent untrusted users from causing OPES services to interfere with the traffic of other users; allow users to see their OPES service profiles and notify them of changes; keep a log of all profile activity for audit purposes; and adhere to a privacy policy guarding users' profiles. The administrator of the decision point is a trusted party and can set policy for individuals or groups using out-of-band communication and configuration files, but users must always be able to query the decision point in order to learn what rules apply to their traffic.

The decision point is responsible for binding identities to the rules and transmitting them to the enforcement point, and the identity it uses for policy decisions must be strictly mapped to the identity the enforcement point uses. If a user goes through an identification and authentication procedure with the decision point and is known there as A, and the enforcement point uses IP addresses for identities, then the decision point must give the enforcement point a binding between A and the user's current IP address. A publishing site may be represented by only a single identity, which makes the authentication and authorisation databases easier for the enforcement point to handle.

Authentication may be necessary between decision points and enforcement points, enforcement points and callout servers, enforcement points and other enforcement points, and callout servers and other callout servers, for the purpose of validating privacy policies. Wherever user data or traffic crosses trust domain boundaries, the originating trust domain should have a policy describing which other domains are trusted, and should authenticate the domains and their policies before forwarding information.

When an individual selects or deselects an OPES service, the individual must be authenticated by the service provider, meaning a binding between the user's communication channel and an identity known to the provider is made in a secure manner. This should be done using a strong authentication method with a public key certificate for the user, which helps in resolving later disputes, and the provider should keep a log of all requests for OPES services and use public key certificates to authenticate responses. Trusted users who may assign, remove or block services for particular users must be authenticated before being allowed to modify the policy base. Because of the sensitivity of user profiles, the interface between the enforcement point and the decision point must use a secure transport protocol, and the enforcement points must adhere to the privacy preferences of the users. Every OPES service must have a unique name for the entity publishing it, that name must be used when notifying users about their service profiles, and there must be a cryptographic binding between the unique name and the entity responsible for the functional behaviour of the service.

On authorisation, users may block particular services so that they are not applied to their traffic, and a block all OPES directive must be supported on a per user basis. A response to a request can be positive or negative, with reasons such as service unknown or service denied by decision point policy, and positive responses should include the identity of the requestor and the service and the type of request. Four cases complicate the decision. If the end user has blocked a service but a trusted user of the decision point wants it applied anyway, the end user should prevail unless there are security or legal reasons to leave it in place. If the publisher and the end user are in the same domain and both are clients of a decision point, the decision point must have policy rules naming the identities allowed to set such rules. If the publisher requests a service for an end user, the decision point must use strong methods to identify the user and their traffic, and the user must be able to request and receive information about the service profile that the publisher's site keeps about them. And if the end user requests a service specific to a publisher's identity while the publisher prohibits the service, the publisher must be able to request and receive profile information that a user keeps about that publisher.
sections.plainLanguage: Users can see what is being applied to their traffic, turn services off, and block them all at once. Publishers can ask for services too, but a user who has said no usually wins, unless there is a legal or security reason not to.

sections.title: Privacy and Integrity
sections.content:
The requests and responses should be cryptographically tied to the identities of the requestor and responder, and the messages should not be alterable without detection. A certificate-based digital signature is strongly recommended as part of the authentication process, and a binding between the request and the response should be established using a well-founded cryptographic means, to show that the response is made in reply to a specific request.

As directed by the enforcement point, content is transformed in whole or in part by OPES services, which means that end-to-end cryptographic protections cannot be used. The memo judges this probably acceptable for the vast majority of traffic, but where a lesser form of content protection is desirable, hop-by-hop protections can be used instead. Integrity using shared secrets must be used between all processing points, end to end in the sense that the two ends of a hop must share a secret, though the secret may differ between hops, and the processing points include the callout servers. Encryption can be requested separately, with the same secret sharing requirement between hops, and when requested it applies to all processing points including callout servers. The signal for integrity, and optionally encryption, must originate from either the requestor, in which case it is applied to the response as well, or the responder, in which case it covers only the response. The shared secrets must be unique, to within a very large probabilistic certainty, for each requestor and responder pair, which helps protect the privacy of end user data from insider attacks or configuration errors while it transits the provider's network.

The decision point must have a privacy policy regarding OPES data such as user profiles for services, and users must be able to limit the promulgation of their profile data and their identities. The supported limitations must include the ability to prevent identity from being given to callout servers, the ability to prevent profile information from being shared, the ability to prevent traffic data from being sent to callout servers run by third parties, and the ability to prevent traffic from particular sites from being given to OPES callout servers.

When an OPES service is provided by a third party, it must have a privacy policy and must identify itself to upstream and downstream parties, telling them how to access that privacy policy. The memo's own security considerations section adds only that the policy, authorisation and enforcement requirements of OPES are discussed in the document and that the security and privacy issues related to OPES services are covered in RFC 3837.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the services rewrite the content, you cannot protect the data from end to end; the protection has to be applied hop by hop instead. And the user can say what may be passed on: their identity, their profile, their traffic to third-party servers, or their traffic to particular sites.

viz.caption: WHAT A SERVICE PROVIDER MUST DO FOR ITS USERS

items.title: Choice
items.text: Users can add, remove or block services for their own traffic

items.title: Isolation
items.text: One user cannot cause services to interfere with another user's traffic

items.title: Visibility
items.text: Users can see their service profile and are told when it changes

items.title: Audit
items.text: A log of all profile activity is kept

items.title: Privacy policy
items.text: The provider follows a policy that guards users' profiles
